brief_extract:
EDINBURGH

—venue for the EAW Annual
Conference

THREE of our most successful and glamorous annual conferences have been held North of the Border. The first and most memor-able to date was the one in Perth on the occasion of our Silver Jubilee in 1950; the second was in Edinburgh in 1958, and the third in Aberdeen in 1964. Now we are looking forward to returning to Scotland in May this year for another conference in Edinburgh which will mark the start of our Golden Jubilee celebrations, and how right and proper this is for a national association whose very first branch was formed in Scotland.

brief_extract: It was, however, in the eighteenth century that so many famous poets, writers, thinkers and artists were gathered together in the city and found opportunities to express their own individual inspiration in their own independent ways. Allan Ramsay, the poet, aided the literary revival by starting the first lending library in Scotland in his book shop in the High Street. Another poet, Robert Fergusson, was the friend and inspiration of Robert Burns, and Burns himself lodged in the Royal Mile for a time and became the idol of Edinburgh society.

brief_context: Gardens where the Scott Monument is located.
brief_extract: The most distinguished perhaps of all Edinburgh's men of letters, Sir Walter Scott, was born and bred in the city, was called to the Bar there and practised as a lawyer as well as producing his vast output of novels and poems. Another famous writer who lived and wrote in Edinburgh was Robert Louis Stevenson who was also called to the Bar and who loved to wander over the Pentland Hills to the south west of the City.

SPOTTED Dick, Roly Poly — such lovely names that make one wonder how such inexpensive yet scrumptious dishes came to be given these names. Dishes such as Hampshire puddings often derived their names from the area in which they were popular, and some like Yorkshire pudding became nationally famous. brief_context: Location where the day centre for the handicapped was built.
brief_extract:
MEETING A NEED

A SURVEY of physically handicapped people in Norwich in 1964 revealed the need for a day centre providing recreational, occupational, social and educational facilities which were not to be found in the existing voluntary organisations. Since some of the latter had difficulty with their accommodation it was even more necessary for the Local Authority to provide premises in which the voluntary organisations could have a part.

brief_extract: Such action, however, serves to emphasise our dependence at the present time on oil products in all aspects of our daily life. article_title: From THE PRESIDENT OF THE ELECTRICAL ASSOCIATION FOR WOMEN, THE COUNTESS DE LA WARR, D.B.E.
brief_extract: I hope that all who attend the Conference will have a happy and memorable time and will enjoy the very generous Scottish hospitality that is coming our way. It is of course right and proper that we should be crossing the Border for the start of our Golden Jubilee celebrations because although our Association was launched in London our very first branch was formed in Glasgow. To those of our members who are not able to be with us in Edinburgh I want to say that I am sure there will be opportunities for each and everyone of them to join in Jubilee celebrations in their own branches and areas during the coming twelve months.

location_standardised: North of Scotland, Scotland, United Kingdom
brief_context: Mentioned regarding the North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board.
article_title: ELECTRICITY IN THE SOUTH OF SCOTLAND
brief_extract: It makes simple sense to the northerner to control at the same time not only the generation and transmission of his power but also the distribution and selling of it. The basic set-up is that the North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board cater for about one and a quarter million people in their 22,000 sq miles of territory while the South of Scotland Electricity Board minister to the electrical needs of about four million people in about 8,000 sq miles. Administratively, there is a dividing line—from the south end of Loch Lomond over to the Firth of Tay—but the Boards work closely together.

brief_context: Used to define the dividing line between electricity boards.
article_title: ELECTRICITY IN THE SOUTH OF SCOTLAND
brief_extract: The basic set-up is that the North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board cater for about one and a quarter million people in their 22,000 sq miles of territory while the South of Scotland Electricity Board minister to the electrical needs of about four million people in about 8,000 sq miles. Administratively, there is a dividing line—from the south end of Loch Lomond over to the Firth of Tay—but the Boards work closely together. Indeed, since mid-1965 the control of electricity generation and future generation planning has been on an all-Scotland basis.

brief_context: Mentioned in context of the nationalised electricity supply industry.
article_title: ELECTRICITY IN THE SOUTH OF SCOTLAND
brief_extract:
The important point is that it is people, and not statistics, that matter: the continuity of supply was not to meters but to about one and a half million consumers. The Board's predecessors were the South East Scotland and the South West Scotland divisions of the then British Electricity Authority, who were responsible for generation and main transmission, and the South East Scotland and South West Scotland Electricity Boards—two
of the area boards established to distribute electricity in Great Britain when the electricity supply industry was nationalised in 1948. The relevant statistics, likewise, can be pruned down to leave a picture of demand virtually doubling every 10 years.

brief_context: Region identified for potential new power station locations.
article_title: ELECTRICITY IN THE SOUTH OF SCOTLAND
brief_extract: This power comes from stations throughout the Board's area—mostly coal-fired but including hydro schemes as well. The SSEB have sought approval in principle from the Secretary of State for Scotland of three locations in Central Scotland identified as potential sites for new power stations. Specifically, the Board consider that Torness Point, near Dunbar on the East coast of Scotland, could accommodate up to two nuclear stations each of 2,640 MW capacity; Chapeldonan, near Girvan on the West coast, could also accommodate up to two nuclear stations each of 2,640 MW capacity; while Carriden, near Bo'ness on the Firth of Forth, could take one gas or oil-fired station of 2,640 MW capacity.

brief_context: Area where water power from lochs was developed.
brief_extract: by GEORGE BANKS, Information Officer, North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board. THE Hydro-Electric Development (Scotland) Bill which set up the North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board in 1943 was a piece of far-sighted planning to be introduced in those war-torn years, and was more than mere legislation to permit the fuller development of a great natural resource, the water-power of Highland lochs and rivers, by a public authority. Primarily, it was designed to improve conditions, to introduce new facilities and comforts to isolated areas, provide opportunity there for initiative and industry and give the Highlands and Islands ‘a future as well as a past’.

location_standardised: Highlands and Islands, Scotland, United Kingdom
brief_context: Region aimed to be improved by hydro-electric development.
brief_extract: THE Hydro-Electric Development (Scotland) Bill which set up the North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board in 1943 was a piece of far-sighted planning to be introduced in those war-torn years, and was more than mere legislation to permit the fuller development of a great natural resource, the water-power of Highland lochs and rivers, by a public authority. Primarily, it was designed to improve conditions, to introduce new facilities and comforts to isolated areas, provide opportunity there for initiative and industry and give the Highlands and Islands ‘a future as well as a past’. The North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board were empowered to carry out all large scale development of water power and to undertake the public supply of electricity in the sparsely populated parts of the North outside the areas of existing private and municipal undertakings.

brief_context: Site of a sod-cutting ceremony in 1945.
brief_extract: These powers and duties and the Board’s area of operation were extended by subsequent legislation. As with so many big jobs there was a sod-cutting ceremony at the start, but this ceremony on the shore of Loch Lomond in 1945 was different. Instead of the traditional polished spade there was an 18-ton bulldozer, the sod was a 12-feet wide strip of turf 100 feet long, and the job, the first step in a continuous drive to build dams, power stations and supply networks throughout the North, was the Loch Sloy hydro-electric scheme whose great dam and power station were to draw visitors from all over the world and become a kind of symbol of post-war Scotland.

Clootie Dumpling from Ayrshire Branch

1 lb flour
2 tsp white breadcrumbs
8 oz shredded suet
8 oz sultanas
8 oz currants
4 oz blue raisins
4 oz chopped peel
8 oz sugar
2 grated apples or carrots
½ tsp salt
1 tsp baking soda
8 oz black treacle
2 tsp each cinnamon and mixed spice and ginger
2 eggs and a little milk as required

Mix the fruit with the dry ingredients. Add the beaten eggs and treacle and enough milk to make a fairly stiff mixture.

brief_context: Mentioned in contrast to Scotland's native plant distribution.

Native Plants
We have so far concentrated on tender plants that can be grown under favourable conditions but what about the native plants for which Scotland is so famous? There is of course the bluebell of Scotland (campanula rotundifolia) which is in England, the harebell, and flowers in July and August. Although it grows on pastures, heaths and banks throughout Britain it is often included in herbaceous borders in our gardens.

brief_context: Setting of the article and location of the Baxter company.
brief_extract:
Twentieth-Century Romance from Speyside
SPEYSIDE—yes, that fair land in North-east Scotland where you can live like a laird on the fine natural foods of this bountiful countryside—salmon from the rushing, tumbling waters of the River Spey, succulent wild duck from the Loch of Spynie, plump pheasant and partridge, hare and prime venison from the sporting estates, soft fruit and vegetables from the fertile Laich of Moray—and all of these have truly been captured for the whole world to enjoy by BAXTERS OF SPEYSIDE throughout their wonderful range of delightful soups, mouth-watering casseroles, canned fruits and jams. That go-ahead company, with its international ramifications, is still a family-owned concern, a rare thing in these days of manufacturing giants and takeover bids.

brief_context: One of the towns visited by William for sales.
brief_extract: William, therefore, approached the local landowner, the Duke of Richmond and Gordon, and secured a plot of land near the Spey on which to build their own small jam factory, and it was indeed a great day for them when they started production there in 1916. Whilst William strove to extend the area of their sales by travelling extensively in the North of Scotland from Wick to Aberdeen his wife took care of the production side of the business at Fochabers—and incidentally, as a matter of interest, this same original small factory is incorporated fully in their establishment today. Ethel was an ingenious person and her range of jams grew to include such delicacies as jellies made from local blaeberries, wild brambles, cranberries, and Little Scarlet Strawberry Jam an exquisite preserve made from the small wild mountain strawberries.

brief_extract:
CRAMOND, Edinburgh

Founded as an outpost of ancient Rome, and for fifteen centuries a bastion of Christianity, Cramond is a seashore suburb of modern Edinburgh. Is there another village that numbers among its visitors a Roman Emperor, a King of Scots and a Queen of the United Kingdom, and all of them leaving their mark?

brief_context: Location of the EAW Golden Jubilee Year conference.
brief_extract: One tends to forget the clouding of the economic sky when such memorable events as the World Cup and Wimbledon occupy our attention. Since jubilation is really related to a jubilee the EAW has had very good cause to celebrate and the excitement all started with the launching of the EAW Golden Jubilee Year at the unforgettable conference in Scotland. Another cause for EAW rejoicing was the award of the CBE to Miss Mary George in the Birthday Honours List.

Mr Kinloch of the National Inspection Council for Electrical Installation Contracting shows how electrical wiring makes its contribution to the home environment.

brief_context: Venue for a reception for branch delegates.
brief_extract: A display of Highland Dancing added to the pleasure. The next evening each of the branch delegates had the great honour of attending a reception at Edinburgh Castle where guests were received by Lord Hughes, Minister of State for Scotland, and Lady Hughes. The Castle was floodlit in honour of the Conference.

brief_context: Location of the Scottish EAW branches and government officials.
brief_extract: For the 800 representatives from the 260 branches the occasion will long be remembered not only for the beauty and historic interest of the city but for the generous hospitality of the Scots. The Conference owed much of its success to the very great kindness and care for detailed arrange-ments made by the South of Scotland Electricity Board, which culminated in the wonderful tours on the third day of the Conference. In the beautiful 18th century Assembly Rooms, the venue for all meetings and most of the social events, the Board had constructed a revolving thistle emblem in honour of the EAW's Golden Jubilee, and this became a focal point where many groups of members met each other.

brief_context: Source of congratulatory message to the EAW.

She also read a message of congratulation and good wishes from the EAW in New Zealand. The Annual Report was presented by Miss Mary George, Director, who showed slides of the highlights of the year's work.

brief_context: Location of a stately home visited by the author.
brief_extract:
KINLOCH, DFH, CEng, MIEE. Assistant Chief Engineer, National Inspection Council for Electrical Installation Contracting

I recently visited a 'stately home' on the edge of the Lake District which was first wired for electricity some 60 years ago. Although the owner was doubtless proud of his pioneering use of electric lighting, he insisted that the whole installation should be completely concealed so that even today there are no visible lighting fittings (or luminaires as they are now called) and even the lighting switches are concealed behind little doors cut in the panelling of the principal rooms.

location_standardised: London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: The specific branch of the EAW that organized the visit.
article_title: VISIT TO LOWER NURSERIES, ROYAL BOTANIC GARDENS, KEW
brief_extract:
P. HARDING, Hon Secretary, London Branch

Electricity is used principally for controls, for irrigation systems and for lighting. The Lower Nursery consists of an aluminium three bay extended eaves glasshouse divided into two sections, a two-bay and a single bay, to cater for differing temperature regimes.

location_standardised: Kew, Richmond, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: A building at Kew Gardens with an associated 17th-century garden.
article_title: VISIT TO LOWER NURSERIES, ROYAL BOTANIC GARDENS, KEW
brief_extract: Since these greenhouses have a 25% changeover each week, a good supply of reserve plants is needed. The second bay consisted of plants for hothouses and the third bay the summer bedding plants required for the outside beds and the 17th century garden at the rear of Key House containing lavender, camomile, rosemary and various herbs, all plants of the period. Ventilation is automatic with the control thermostat mounted in the same spot as the heating thermostat to avoid any local temperature disparity.

brief_extract:
Going to the Palace
by MARY GEORGE, CBE, Companion IEE, Director EAW
'WHAT was it like at the Palace?' 'Did you have the Queen?' 'What was she wear- ing?' These are some of the questions that are asked of the fortunate ones called to an Investiture. I went to Buckingham Palace to receive my CBE on one of those grey overcast mornings typical of this summer. We were instructed to arrive between 10.00 am and 10.30 am and of course we were all early.

location_standardised: The Mall, London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: The road where vehicles queued to enter the Palace.
brief_extract: We were instructed to arrive between 10.00 am and 10.30 am and of course we were all early. Just as well as we had to queue up in the Mall to have our cars searched for bombs—it was one of those periods. When we were cleared we advanced slowly past the gaping crowds through the splendid wrought iron gates of the Palace into the Forecourt.

location_standardised: Buckingham Palace, London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Area inside the Palace gates.
brief_extract: Just as well as we had to queue up in the Mall to have our cars searched for bombs—it was one of those periods. When we were cleared we advanced slowly past the gaping crowds through the splendid wrought iron gates of the Palace into the Forecourt. Here we were stopped by a very polite young police- man who asked us if we had had our boots examined.

location_standardised: Buckingham Palace, London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: A room guests pass through.
brief_extract: We had really arrived. We follow everyone else to the Grand En- trance with its two-storied portico, up a short flight of steps and into the Grand Hall. Now we have to follow directions.

location_standardised: Buckingham Palace, London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: The stairs guests take to reach the Ball Room.
brief_extract: Soon we are parted from our friends. Visitors go up the Grand Staircase and make their way to the Ball Room where they are able to settle down, relax and listen to the band until the Queen arrives. The recipient, if she is a woman, may now be faced with her one and only decision of the morning; does she leave her coat in the cloakroom or does she keep it on?

location_standardised: London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Where the testing house was first established in 1948.
brief_extract: Then we learned the history of ATL. The Electricity Supply Industry's testing house was first established in London by the Electrical Development Association (EDA) in 1948, and since the working facilities were inadequate as the work increased, a new laboratory was built at Leatherhead in 1953. The Industry was nationalised in 1948 but the laboratory remained independent until 1964 when the Electricity Council took over the responsibility, and in 1966 introduced a new section for performance testing.

location_standardised: Downend, South Gloucestershire, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Destination of the return journey after the lab visit.
article_title: Visit to the Appliance Testing Laboratories (Continued)
brief_extract: Time was too short to allow us to see other laboratories where commercial appliances were tested or where thermostats, energy regulators and time switches come under close scrutiny. As we made our return journey to Downend there were many new facts running through our minds and although we may not all have been able to fully answer questions like—a busy housewife may drop an electric iron—will it shatter? A finger may be poked through an opening in an appliance—will it reach live parts?
